content: Idiopathic short stature (ISS) is a condition in which children are significantly shorter than their peers for reasons that are either unknown or hereditary. Recombinant human growth hormone (GH) has been utilized as a treatment to promote growth and improve final adult height in children diagnosed with ISS. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of recombinant human GH on both short-term growth and final height in children with ISS. To achieve this, researchers conducted a systematic review of randomized controlled trials (RCTs). These studies were identified through comprehensive searches of databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, The Cochrane Library, Science Citation Index, BIOSIS, and Current Controlled Trials. Additionally, reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed, and experts and pharmaceutical companies were consulted to identify further trials. The inclusion criteria for the studies were as follows: participants had to be children with ISS who demonstrated normal GH secretion. The treatment involved administering recombinant GH for a minimum duration of six months, and the outcomes had to be compared with either a placebo or no treatment. The studies needed to assess growth or height as an outcome measure. Two reviewers independently evaluated the studies for inclusion and methodological quality. Data extraction was performed by one reviewer and verified by another. The primary outcome of interest was final height, while secondary outcomes included short-term growth, health-related quality of life, and adverse effects. When appropriate, data were pooled using a random-effects model to estimate overall treatment effects. A total of ten RCTs were included in the analysis. One trial specifically examined near-final height in girls and found that those treated with GH were, on average, 7.5 cm taller than untreated controls (mean height in the GH group: 155.3 cm ± 6.4; mean height in the control group: 147.8 cm ± 2.6; P = 0.003). Another trial reported adult height standard deviation scores and demonstrated that children treated with GH were, on average, 3.7 cm taller than those in the placebo group (95% confidence interval: 0.03 to 1.10; P < 0.04). Other trials primarily reported short-term outcomes, with findings suggesting that short-term height gains could range from negligible to approximately 0.7 standard deviations over one year. One study assessed health-related quality of life and found no significant improvement in children treated with GH compared to those in the control group. Similarly, another study found no substantial evidence that GH treatment influenced psychological adaptation or self-perception in children with ISS. Importantly, no serious adverse effects associated with GH treatment were reported in the included studies. In conclusion, GH therapy has been shown to increase short-term growth and improve near-final or final height in children with ISS. However, even with treatment, these children often remain relatively short compared to peers of average stature. Further large-scale, multicenter RCTs are needed to better evaluate the impact of GH therapy on final height, quality of life, and cost-effectiveness.
